_note: Generated by scripts/build-build-log.mjs from recorded trade-offs, failed approaches, lessons and limitations in the case studies. Not hand-authored: there are no invented entries here, and no entry carries a date because the registry does not record one. Dates will appear as `lastVerifiedAt` coverage grows; until then the log is ordered by kind and project rather than pretending to a chronology it cannot support.

entries.body: Never progressed past a prototype; the source was removed from the ecosystem during the 2026-08 migration and this write-up survives as provenance.

entries.title: Porting the predecessor's analytics Web Worker, which used `eval()` to evaluate derived metrics.
entries.body: Evaluating strings at runtime in a worker was an unnecessary code-execution surface for something that only ever needed a fixed set of calculations.
entries.change: The worker was not ported. Arise uses safe in-thread helpers instead, and the issue is documented in the archived predecessor's README as part of the porting log.

entries.title: No cloud sync — versioned file export instead
entries.body: Moving between devices is a manual export and import. Gained: No account, no backend, and the user owns the backup file outright.

entries.title: Deliberately no nutrition system
entries.body: The training/nutrition loop most competitors sell is out of scope by design. Gained: Arise stays a training product rather than becoming a second copy of Forq.

Porting an old project is a chance to leave things behind. The predecessor is kept as a frozen, read-only mirror purely for provenance, which made it easy to be explicit about what was deliberately not carried forward.
Progression prescriptions are backtested internally; they have never been compared against coach-written programmes.
No training-outcome data exists — 'works' currently means the tests pass and loads compute, not that users got stronger.
The 1–20 attribute curve is authored judgement, not fitted to data.

entries.title: Naming credible institutions instead of implying live citations
entries.body: The user has to do the research themselves; the app cannot hand them the article. Gained: The app never presents a fabricated link as a source, which is the standard failure of AI-generated debate prompts.

entries.title: Voice input via the browser Web Speech API
entries.body: Chrome-family browsers only; everywhere else the composer silently falls back to typing. Gained: Dictation and read-aloud with no service dependency and no cost.
Judge-scoring invariance is validated on synthetic transcripts; there is no inter-rater agreement study against human judges yet.
Rate limiting is process-local; running multiple instances would need shared state the current design does not have.
PvP assumes small trusted cohorts; anti-abuse beyond rate limits is thin.

entries.title: Hosted transcription by default with an optional local model
entries.body: The default path sends audio off the machine, which is why privacy mode and the offline fallback both exist. Gained: Fast, accurate and near-free transcription without shipping a multi-gigabyte model.

entries.title: Windows-native, with documented notes for macOS and Linux
entries.body: Cross-platform support is best-effort rather than first-class. Gained: The focused-window paste behaviour actually works properly on the primary platform.
A personal utility, never hardened for distribution; its source was removed during the 2026-08 ecosystem migration.

entries.title: Start empty rather than seed a demo
entries.body: A much weaker first impression. The app has almost nothing to show until real data goes in, which is a genuine adoption cost. Gained: Every figure the user sees is about them, and there is no cliff when demo data is cleared.

entries.title: Model the pantry as approximate rather than exact
entries.body: Precise inventory and exact cost accounting are out of reach — the numbers are ranges and estimates, and the UI has to say so. Gained: Coverage and expiry work with the way people actually track food, so the recommender stays useful on messy data.

entries.title: Deliberately not building a full nutrition system
entries.body: Nutrition remains an overview rather than a feature, which rules out a whole category of users. Gained: Forq stays a planning and shopping product, and does not become a second copy of a tracking app.
Progressive disclosure is only honest if hiding a module provably keeps its records. Without that guarantee, 'simplify the interface' and 'lose your data' look identical from the outside.
Pantry confidence is user-entered, so recommendations inherit guessing rather than correcting it.
Cost and nutrition figures come from authored recipe data, not retailer APIs — prices drift from reality.
Single-household model; local-first storage means no multi-user conflict handling.

entries.title: 100% client-side with a user-supplied API key
entries.body: The user has to obtain and paste their own key, which is a hard first step for a non-technical learner. Gained: No backend, no accounts, no cost to run, and the key never leaves the user's browser.
No learner-progress study exists; fluency improvement is not measured and is graded 'insufficient-evidence' in the ecosystem's evidence registry.
Groq STT/TTS correction accuracy has never been benchmarked.
The API key lives in localStorage by design for a private tool — not hardened for public deployment.

entries.title: Electron desktop app alongside the web dashboard
entries.body: A desktop install, a second codebase, and Windows-native audio handling that does not transfer to other platforms for free. Gained: System-audio capture, which a browser cannot do.
Built for personal meetings and never operated at scale; its source was removed during the 2026-08 ecosystem migration.

entries.title: Join code as the entire identity model
entries.body: The join code is the only thing protecting the board, which the project's own README documents as a security limitation rather than glossing over. Gained: A household is usable in under a minute, with no sign-up friction for the partner who did not choose the app.

entries.title: No score and no leaderboard
entries.body: The engagement mechanics that would make it stickier are exactly the ones that would make it harmful here. Gained: The tool makes invisible work visible without giving either person a number to win with.
Some products are defined by what you refuse to add. A fairness percentage would have been trivial to compute and would have changed what the app is for.
No external pentest; RLS isolation is exercised by the integration suite only.
Invitation tokens are hashed but brute-force resistance is not load-tested.
Two-person scope is a product decision, not an enforced guarantee — any household member sees everything.

entries.title: Deterministic core owns every number; the model is confined to prose
entries.body: Evaluation is limited to features that can be counted from a transcript, so it cannot judge the things a human coach would notice but cannot count. Gained: Scores are reproducible and testable, the app degrades to full functionality with no provider, and a model outage cannot change anyone's mastery.

entries.title: Onboarding produces priors with wide uncertainty instead of a score
entries.body: A less satisfying first run. There is no number to show off on day one, which is exactly what most competing products lead with. Gained: The app never hands someone a label off seven questions, and confidence genuinely grows with evidence.

entries.title: Local-first with every permission off by default
entries.body: No cross-device continuity without deliberate setup, and no aggregate data to improve the model with. Gained: Sensitive practice material stays on device; sync, when enabled, stores only an opaque encrypted blob.

Tracking mastery and confidence as one number collapses two different things — knowing how to do something and believing you can — and the product's whole reason to exist lives in the gap between them.
No longitudinal field study — transfer from simulator practice to real conversations is asserted by the design, never measured.
The human-rated evaluation pipeline holds zero external ratings so far.
The safety gate is deterministic pattern matching; no third-party adversarial red-team has audited it.

entries.title: One deep pipeline instead of a breadth tracker with dashboards
entries.body: No correlations, no trends across symptoms, none of the breadth that makes a tracker feel comprehensive. Gained: The product does one thing that other tools do not do at all: challenge the interpretation rather than record the mood.

entries.title: Enforcing the language contract in a validator rather than in the prompt
entries.body: Rejected responses mean occasional dead ends and retries, and the contract has to be maintained alongside every prompt change. Gained: A model that drifts cannot ship a diagnosis to the user — the response is rejected before it renders.
When the biggest product risk is a sentence, the sentence needs a type and a validator. Prompt instructions are a preference; a rejection is a guarantee.
No user study and no clinician review of the hedged language the pipeline produces.
Bias-flag thresholds (confidence ≥ 0.45) are engineering choices, not clinically validated cut-offs.
Longitudinal calibration assumes follow-up answers are self-reported honestly.
The upstream CI workflow file was removed from the emotion-tracker repository on 2026-08-22; the stage-beta label rests on the last green run (2026-08-21) until it is restored.

entries.title: Topic-level provenance on curriculum content, with statement-level coverage computed on top of it.
entries.body: Coverage was reported per statement but provenance was only recorded per topic, so the claim that every examinable statement was individually mapped was not actually true of the data.
entries.change: Every spec point across all four science and maths curriculum files was migrated to carry its own verification, source, reviewer, last-checked date and spec version, so the reported coverage now reflects verification rather than mere presence.

entries.title: Local-first IndexedDB as the default, sync as an opt-in
entries.body: Cross-device revision is not available out of the box, which is a real cost for someone revising on both a laptop and a phone. Gained: The app works with zero setup and no account, and a student's data never leaves their machine unless they ask for it.

entries.title: Curriculum as validated data modules rather than hardcoded content
entries.body: Considerably more up-front work than hardcoding one syllabus, and every content change now has to satisfy the validator. Gained: New boards and qualifications are additive, and a validator can enforce provenance and density floors across all of them.
A coverage number is only as honest as the granularity of the metadata underneath it. Reporting statement-level coverage from topic-level provenance quietly overstated what had been checked.
No external examiner blind study — marking agreement is measured against an internal double-marked corpus only.
Short-answer formats only; maths/LaTeX equivalence checking is internal.
FSRS scheduling ships library defaults; retention has never been studied inside the product.

entries.title: Per-tool parsers instead of one general-purpose compressor
entries.body: Every new tool needs its own parser. Unrecognised output falls back to generic structural compression and does noticeably less well. Gained: Reduction of 99% or better on the synthetic fixtures that dominate the benchmark. Captured real transcripts are still in single digits, so the figure has not yet been shown on production-shaped input.

entries.title: Deterministic synthetic fixtures rather than recorded real-world logs
entries.body: Fixtures are shaped like real output but are not real output, so the numbers describe representative cases rather than a measured production workload. Gained: The benchmark is reproducible by anyone, runs in CI, and its numbers can be regenerated on demand.
Publishing a reduction percentage without a retention percentage next to it would have made the tool look better and be less trustworthy. Pairing the two is what makes the number worth anything.
The benchmark corpus is internally curated tool output; no independent corpus exists.
LLM task-success was measured on narrow rtk-specific fixtures, not general agentic workflows.
Redaction covers common secret shapes by construction; novel formats pass through.

entries.title: Locking the whole app down with a strict Content-Security-Policy
entries.body: The globe renders through a three.js WebGL canvas, which cannot run under a strict CSP — every lockdown attempt broke the map that is the product. The monorepo improvement log records the outcome directly: "CSP deferred — globe `three`/`canvas` breaks on strict CSP."
entries.change: Security headers shipped without a CSP and the absence was recorded as an explicit known limitation, rather than shipping a policy that looked enforced while the app silently bypassed it.

entries.title: Story clusters instead of one summary per country
entries.body: A country page is denser and slower to read than a three-paragraph summary would be. Gained: Disagreement between sources survives into the interface, which is the whole point of the product.

entries.title: Named credible institutions rather than live-fetched citations on the debate-style grounding path
entries.body: Those are starting points, not live citations — and the README says so rather than implying the app fetched them. Gained: The user gets real, well-known places to go and research, instead of plausible-looking fake links.

entries.title: Aggressive caching on free API tiers
entries.body: Country pages can be up to six hours stale, which is a real limitation for fast-moving events. Gained: The app runs at near-zero cost and stays within daily quotas.
The honest version of an AI news product is mostly plumbing for provenance. The generation step is the easy part; carrying source, conflict and absence through to the interface is the work.
Free-tier API quotas capped freshness — country pages could be six hours stale by design.
A strict Content-Security-Policy was abandoned because three.js cannot run under one.
The source was removed during the 2026-08 ecosystem migration; no further verification of these claims is possible.
